content: Corundum, derived from the Tamil words kurundam or kuruvindam, is a crystalline form of aluminum oxide and is classified as one of the rock-forming minerals. In its pure state, corundum is transparent, but the presence of impurities can impart various colors to the mineral. Transparent specimens of corundum are used as gemstones. When the gemstone is red, it is referred to as a ruby, while all other colors are classified as sapphires. A specific variety of sapphire with a pinkish-orange hue is known as padparadscha. Corundum is exceptionally hard, with a Mohs hardness of 9, making it capable of scratching nearly all other minerals. When used to scratch other minerals, it leaves a white streak. This hardness makes corundum a valuable abrasive material, utilized in applications ranging from sandpaper to large industrial machines for machining metals, plastics, and wood. Its density is approximately 4.02 g/cm³, which is notably high for a transparent mineral composed of the low atomic mass elements aluminum and oxygen. Corundum is found as a mineral in metamorphic rocks such as mica schist, gneiss, and certain marbles. It also occurs in low-silica igneous rocks like syenite and nepheline syenite intrusions. Other occurrences include masses near ultramafic intrusions, associations with lamprophyre dikes, and large crystals within pegmatites. Due to its hardness and resistance to weathering, corundum is often found as a detrital mineral in stream and beach sands. Corundum used for abrasives is mined in countries such as Zimbabwe, Russia, and India. Historically, it was also extracted from deposits associated with dunites in North Carolina and from nepheline syenite in Craigmont, Ontario. Emery-grade corundum is found on the Greek island of Naxos and near Peekskill, New York. Additionally, abrasive corundum is synthetically manufactured from bauxite. Synthetic Corundum The first synthetic rubies were created in 1837 by Gaudin, who fused alumina at high temperatures with a small amount of chromium as a pigment. In 1847, Edelman produced white sapphire by fusing alumina in boric acid. By 1877, Frenic and Freil succeeded in producing crystal corundum from which small stones could be cut. Later, Frimy and Auguste Verneuil manufactured artificial rubies by fusing barium fluoride (BaF₂) and aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) with a small amount of chromium at temperatures exceeding 2000°C. In 1903, Verneuil announced the ability to produce synthetic rubies on a commercial scale using the flame fusion process. The Verneuil process enables the production of flawless single-crystal sapphires, rubies, and other corundum gemstones in sizes much larger than those typically found in nature. Additionally, gem-quality synthetic corundum can be grown using flux-growth and hydrothermal synthesis methods. The simplicity of these synthetic methods has led to the availability of large quantities of synthetic corundum on the market, significantly reducing their cost in recent years. Beyond ornamental uses, synthetic corundum is employed in the production of mechanical components such as tubes, rods, bearings, and other machined parts. It is also used to create scratch-resistant watch crystals, windows for optical equipment, spacecraft, and laser components.
